# Worksheet: your first Julia model code

**~45 minutes**

This is the first worksheet of the workshop and it assumes you have never
written Julia before. Everything here uses the SIR model exactly as the session
presented it. Nothing new is asked of you epidemiologically. What is new is the
Julia: writing a model kernel (the function that computes the rates of change),
broadcasting a calculation over a grid, drawing a figure, and generating random
numbers you can reproduce.

You will not *solve* anything today. Turning these ingredients into an epidemic
curve is the next two sessions' job; this one is about writing the code they
will need.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Parts A and B are the session.** **Part C** goes further if you get there; not
reaching it is completely fine. Worked solutions are posted at the end of each
day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

::: {.callout-important}
## The first cell is slow — that is normal

The first `using CairoMakie` in a fresh session can take a minute or more while
Julia compiles the plotting stack. It is not frozen, and it only happens once
per session. Later cells run quickly.
:::

**Coming from R?** Most of what you know transfers.

| R | Julia | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `f <- function(x) x^2` | `f(x) = x^2` | or `function f(x) ... end` |
| `x <- c(1, 2, 3)` | `x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]` | `1.0` and `1` are different types |
| `v[1]` | `v[1]` | indexing starts at 1, as in R |
| `sapply(v, f)` | `f.(v)` | the dot applies `f` elementwise |
| `x[x < 0.5]` | `x[x .< 0.5]` | comparisons need the dot too |
| `list(a = 1, b = 2)` | `(a = 1, b = 2)` | a named tuple; read fields with `p.a` |
| `TRUE` / `FALSE` | `true` / `false` | lowercase |

**The REPL is your other window.** Alongside this document you have a Julia
prompt. Besides the ordinary `julia>` prompt it has three other modes. Type the
character at an empty prompt to enter one, `Backspace` to leave:

| Key | Mode | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `?` | help | you want a function's arguments — `?expm1` |
| `]` | package | a package seems missing — `]st` also names the active environment |
| `;` | shell | you need `ls` or `git status` without switching windows |

If `using CairoMakie` fails, that is almost always Julia started outside the
project. Check the name in front of the `pkg>` prompt, and ask. This is exactly
the kind of thing an instructor can fix in ten seconds.

Two Julia-specific conventions used throughout the course:

- **Greek letters are ordinary variable names.** We write `β`, `γ`, `λ` because
  they match the equations. Type them with a backslash and Tab: `\beta`↹ gives
  `β`, `\gamma`↹ gives `γ`, `\lambda`↹ gives `λ`. Plain ASCII names work exactly
  as well if you prefer them.
- **A trailing `!`** (as in `sir_ode!`) marks a function that *modifies* one of
  its arguments instead of returning a new value. Nothing enforces this; it is
  a promise to the reader.

## Setup

Run this first. It loads the two packages the worksheet needs and defines the
`check` helper used by every part.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-p01-setup
using CairoMakie
using StableRNGs

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

println("Julia version: ", VERSION)
```

---

## Part A — writing a model kernel (~15 min)

The session's `sir_ode!` had the signature every SciML solver expects:

```julia
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
```

It *writes* the rates of change into `du` rather than returning them. You will
use this shape in every remaining session, so it is worth typing once by hand
rather than only reading.

These are the session's equations, unchanged. The force of infection is
$\lambda = \beta c I / N$, and

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\lambda S, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda S - \gamma I, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} = \gamma I.
$$

Your job is only to turn the second and third of them into Julia. The first is
done for you as a worked example of the pattern.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-p01-a1
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]      # S, I, R

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N        # force of infection, λ = βcI/N
    du[1] = -λ * S                 # dS/dt — worked for you
    du[2] = 0.0     # TODO: replace 0.0 — dI/dt
    du[3] = 0.0     # TODO: replace 0.0 — dR/dt
    return nothing
end

du = zeros(3)
sir_ode!(du, u0, p, 0.0)

check("infectious are increasing", du[2] > 0)
check("people are recovering", du[3] > 0)
check("nobody is created or destroyed",
      any(!iszero, du) && isapprox(sum(du), 0.0; atol = 1e-12))
du
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A

```julia
du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I
du[3] = p.γ * I
```

Note `p.γ` rather than a bare `γ`: the recovery rate arrived inside `p`, and only
`λ` was unpacked for you. `S`, `I` and `R` *were* unpacked, on the first line of
the function, which is why they can be used bare.

The three lines should sum to zero: every term that leaves one compartment
appears with the opposite sign in another. If the conservation check fails, look
for a sign or a missing term.

`zeros(3)` created `du` before the function ran, and the function filled it in.
That is what "in place" means, and it is why `du` holds your answer *after* the
call even though the function returns `nothing`.
:::

### A1. Interpret

These are questions about the Julia, not the epidemiology.

- The function writes `du[2] = ...` rather than `du = [...]`. What would go wrong
  if you built a new array inside the function instead?
- The function ends with `return nothing`, so it hands nothing back. Where did
  your answer end up, and how did it get out?
- The parameters arrived as `p` and you read them with `p.β`. What would break if
  you had used `p[1]` and later reordered the parameters?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part B — the same calculation over a whole grid (~15 min)

A *rate* says how often something happens per unit time; a *probability* says how
likely it is within a window. The session gave the conversion between them for a
window of width $\delta t$:

$$
p(r, \delta t) = 1 - e^{-r\,\delta t}.
$$

You will need this every time a model takes discrete time steps. It is often
replaced by the much simpler $r\,\delta t$, and here you will see for yourself
when that shortcut is safe and when it is not.

Rather than looping over values of $\delta t$, Julia applies a function to an
entire array at once when you add a dot: `f.(v)`. This is the `sapply` of Julia,
but it compiles to a single loop with no intermediate copies.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-p01-b1
rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)   # numerically stable 1 - exp(-r δt)

δts = 0.0:0.25:10.0
γ   = 0.25      # the session's recovery rate, per day

linear = γ .* δts    # the shortcut, elementwise — note the dot on the `*`
probs  = Float64[]   # TODO: replace this — rate_to_proportion at rate γ, for every δt in δts

check("one value of each for every δt",
      length(probs) == length(δts) && length(linear) == length(δts))
check("every probability stays between 0 and 1",
      !isempty(probs) && all(0 .<= probs .<= 1))
check("the shortcut escapes [0, 1]", !isempty(linear) && maximum(linear) > 1)
check("the two agree when δt is small",
      length(probs) > 1 && length(linear) > 1 &&
      isapprox(probs[2], linear[2]; rtol = 0.05))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B

```julia
probs = rate_to_proportion.(γ, δts)
```

The dot goes between the function name and the opening bracket. `γ` is a single
number and `δts` is an array, so Julia reuses `γ` for every element rather than
requiring two arrays of matching length.

The `linear` line above shows the other place dots appear: `γ .* δts` multiplies
elementwise. Once you are broadcasting, the dot goes on operators as well as on
function calls.

To type `δts`, use `\delta`↹ then `ts`, or copy it from the line above.
:::

Now draw them. A figure is built up in pieces: a `Figure` to hold everything, an
`Axis` inside it, then one call per thing you want drawn.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-p01-rate
#| fig-cap: "Probability of at least one event in a window of width δt at rate γ = 0.25, against the linear shortcut γ δt."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "window width δt (days)", ylabel = "probability")
hlines!(ax, [1.0]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "probability = 1")
lines!(ax, δts, linear; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "shortcut γ δt")

# TODO: draw the exact curve — lines!(ax, xvalues, yvalues; linewidth = 3, label = "1 - exp(-γ δt)")

axislegend(ax; position = :rb)
ylims!(ax, 0, 2.6)
fig
```

### B1. Interpret

- Up to roughly which $\delta t$ are the two curves hard to tell apart, and where
  do they part company?
- The shortcut climbs past 1 and keeps going. A probability cannot do that, so
  what quantity is $\gamma\,\delta t$ actually measuring?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part C — random numbers you can reproduce (optional)

*Start this only if you have finished Part B.*

Later sessions simulate epidemics that are genuinely random. Results still have
to be reproducible: the same script must give the same figure on your machine
and on a reviewer's. Julia's answer is a *local* random number generator that you
seed yourself, rather than a hidden global one.

Feed the force of infection from Part A into the conversion from Part B, with a
window of one day, and you get the probability that a given susceptible person is
infected today.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-p01-c1
λ0 = p.β * p.c * u0[2] / p.N          # force of infection at the start
p_infect = rate_to_proportion(λ0, 1.0)

# A seed fixes the entire stream of numbers that follows.
draws_a = rand(StableRNG(2024), 5)
draws_b = rand(StableRNG(2024), 5)
draws_c = rand(StableRNG(99), 5)

check("the same seed gives identical draws", draws_a == draws_b)
check("a different seed gives different draws", draws_a != draws_c)

function infected_today(rng, n_susceptible, p_infect)
    draws = rand(rng, n_susceptible)
    return 0    # TODO: replace 0 — how many of `draws` came out below p_infect?
end

today = infected_today(StableRNG(1), 990, p_infect)
println("of 990 susceptibles, ", today, " are infected today")

# The same experiment repeated a million times, to check the machinery.
fraction = infected_today(StableRNG(2), 1_000_000, p_infect) / 1_000_000
check("the observed fraction matches the probability",
      isapprox(fraction, p_infect; rtol = 0.05))
(; p_infect, fraction, today)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C

```julia
return count(draws .< p_infect)
```

`draws .< p_infect` compares every element against the same number and gives an
array of `true`/`false`, the dot again doing elementwise work. `count` then
counts the `true`s.

If you get a single `true` or `false` rather than a number, you left the dot out
of `<` and compared the whole array at once.
:::

### C1. Interpret

- Run the `today` line again with a few different seeds. Roughly how much does
  the number move? The deterministic model of Part A would give one fixed answer.
  Which is right?
- Why seed a generator you create yourself rather than calling `rand` and
  setting a global seed once at the top of the script?

> *Your answer here.*

## Finish: render your own report

In a terminal, from the top of the repository:

```bash
quarto render worksheets/prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd
```

This runs every cell top to bottom in a fresh session and produces an HTML file
next to the worksheet. A clean render is the same standard you would apply to a
reproducible analysis of your own. It proves the document does not depend on
anything you typed and forgot about.
